medium.titulo: Will Claude Dashboards Replace Power BI and Tableau? I Tested to find it out
medium.resumo: I built a dashboard in Claude in 3 prompts, read what other analysts are saying and what is my take on this.
medium.conteudo_html:
I built a dashboard in Claude in 3 prompts, read what other analysts are saying and what is my take on this.

Three prompts, 5 tabs, and in minutes a presentable dashboard was right in front of me. The pace at which Claude is analyzing the data and creating the dashboard is a game changer.

I tested Claude dashboard on a supply chain dataset, and I had this thought running in my mind that, Is this the end of Power BI or Tableau ? I wanted a real answer because a lot of analysts have different takes. So I did three things. I built a dashboard myself, read everything I could find from analysts and data teams who have tested it since the launch, and compared it against what I know from years of working with enterprise BI tools, Power BI & Tableau.

My Test Setup

To test the dashboard, I utilized the DataCo Smart Supply Chain dataset from Kaggle. It has over 180,000 records and mirrors almost a real enterprise supply chain dataset across orders, sales, product categories, shipping performances, late delivery flags and payment fraud markers.

I chose this specifically because of how realistic the data is and since these data comes with inherent business questions like

Which shipping route drive late deliveries? What is the financial impact and where are the bottlenecks?

Here is what the dashboard looks like. (Showcasing only the first 2 tabs to give an idea)

What Worked?

  1. Unmatched speed to the first draft: In just 3 prompts I had a 5 tab interactive presentable dashboard covering order velocity, late delivery breakdowns, and regional performance. What would normally take half a day of data prep, ideation, chart selection, and layout alignment in Power BI, happened in just 3 prompts. If you have ever started off with a blank canvas in a BI tool, this step actually eliminates that paralysis entirely.
  2. SQL Code Validation: While connecting to live data warehouses, clicking into any KPI cards or visual and that will give you the underlying SQL query. As someone who has spent years in analytics, my first question with any AI output is always , “How can I test or validate this number ?” Being able to audit the raw SQL directly inside the interface itself is a massive win from a transparency standpoint. P.S. This feature is only limited to live database connections only, not csv or excel uploads.
  3. Timely refresh and collaboration : The dashboard is refreshed in real time and every chart shows when it was last refreshed. You can also share the dashboard via the shareable link and your team can collaboratively chat right inside the dashboard for any UX/UI changes or discuss business questions as well. For quick discussions with stakeholders and internal team members, this creates a seamless workflow that I haven’t seen in traditional BI tools.

What Fell Short?

  1. Formatting Polish and Layout Consistency : While functional, the initial output missed some of the aesthetics that a business dashboard has. Grid alignment was inconsistent, borders varied across different sections and Claude defaulted to creation of more of bar charts and tables with excess white spaces. Even after applying a custom color palette, several visuals required reprompting to look presentation ready . If you are handing this to your stakeholders or leadership, expect to spend time on polish.
  2. The Confident Guessing on the KPI logic: Claude was overly confident in defining key business metrics on its own. It generated calculations for metrics without even asking the end user to confirm on the logic . In enterprise analytics, every business unit defines KPIs slightly different. A confident guess that looks right on the surface could be the most dangerous kind of error in executive reporting. This single finding helped me understand what things I need to keep in mind before creating a dashboard using Claude.

What I Dug into after the test?

Just creating a simple dashboard isn’t enough to test this feature. So went through the analysis of other analytics experts and started looking for patterns . Four things kept coming up :

  1. The speed is real, but with a ceiling : A creator mentioned that he was able to create a multi page dashboard in minutes with all sorts of checks done under 15 minutes. I feel the speed pays off the most when stakes are low like exploring data, testing, prepping for a meeting. For a board deck, the hours you save are irrelevant next to one wrong figure. So testing the figures is a must.
  2. The same question can yield to different answers : This concerns the most since AI is probabilistic in nature. So if two people ask the same question, there is high chance that Claude will give two different answers. For example , if you ask Claude, ‘show me late deliveries’. Claude doesn’t know your company’s definition of late — if it is 1 day , past the promised date ? 3 days or 5. So it guesses and writes a SQL query based on that guess. Now your colleague asks the same question and Claude guesses again and suggests something different. You both create a chart of late deliveries but the numbers don’t match . In traditional BI tools, we solve this by defining a metric onece and every dashboard uses the same definition. Claude doesn’t have this layer. But to avoid this what you can do is provide the business logic upfront in the prompt itself for each KPI and after the creation of the dashboard, retest the logic once again to avoid any mistakes.
  3. Governance decides whether companies can use it : Dashboards built in Claude currently lack version control, certification, owners, audit trails, and code export. There is also a data security concern. When you connect a warehouse to Claude, your data leaves your infrastructure and is processed by Anthropic’s servers. On certain plans, that processing happens in the US. If your data include customer PII, financal records, or anything regulated, that is a potential leak vector your security team needs to evaluate before you connect anything.
  4. Analytics is evolving from building to reviewing: When a tool builds a dashboard from a prompt, the value of dragging fields onto axes, formatting, creating calculations, etc drops. What rises instead is reading SQL, understanding table relationships, catching non unique ID, understanding the data model, knowing the business logic.

The pattern that we saw : excellent on speed, weak on trust.

Claude Dashboards vs Enterprise BI Tools (Power BI & Tableau)

So will it replace BI tools?

It will definitely change the ways of working, change where the work starts and not where it ends.

  • It replaces the first draft: Claude removes the blank page problem. Protyping and creating the first draft can be created using Claude but the dashboard your CFO wants to read needs access rules, proper definitions, owner, and a change history. That is what governed BI provides.
  • A semantic layer makes Claude stronger: Running Claude on top of a governed Power BI model is where you get Claude’s speed with the team’s trusted defintions and data. That combination is where we are heading.
  • It’s in beta and the gaps are buildable. I would revisit in couple of months and be careful about concluding anything today.

How I would use it today ?

  • Use it for : exploring a new dataset , quick answers, prototyping, one time analysis.
  • Don’t use it for : official company reporting, sensitive and regulated data, or dashboards many people depend on.
  • Confirm on KPI definitions : Before sharing a dashboard, I would confirm on the numbers and logic behind every KPI and number, confirm with the business owner, check the SQL query, verify data source, check last refresh timing and share consciously.

My takeaway

Claude Dashboards is the fastest way to bridge from data to the first drafty. But speed isn’t trust. Enterprise BI tools have earned their place by solving governance, security and access standards and those problems aren’t going anywhere. So utilise Claude to start faster and use your BI tool to make it official, and don’t skip the step of testing the numbers.

Thank you for reading the blog. ❤

medium.titulo: A 25-Year Crypto Mystery, Solved in 30 Minutes. It Was Just Timestamps.
medium.resumo: How Claude found where the NIST curve seeds came from, and what engineers can learn from the way it looked.
medium.conteudo_html:
How Claude found where the NIST curve seeds came from, and what engineers can learn from the way it looked.

For more than 25 years, a few numbers bothered a lot of smart people.

They sit inside some of the most used security standards on the internet.

Nobody could say where they came from.

This month, that question finally got an answer.

And the answer was boring in the best way.

The numbers nobody could explain

In 2000, NIST published a set of standard elliptic curves. NIST is the US agency that writes many security standards.

You use these curves every day, even if you never see them. P-256 is the famous one.

An elliptic curve here is just a math shape that lets two computers sign and check messages safely.

Each curve came with a “seed.” A seed is a starting number. You hash it, and the result sets part of the curve.

The seeds were supplied by the NSA, with no explanation.

For P-256, the seed was this:

C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90

No note. No method. Just the number.

Why people worried

If you don’t know where a number came from, you can’t rule out that someone picked it on purpose.

The fear was simple. Maybe the NSA tried many seeds until it found a curve with a weakness only it knew about.

People call that a backdoor.

The worry got sharper because of Dual EC, a different NSA-linked random number standard that was widely reported to have a backdoor. It wasn’t these curves. But it made people careful.

Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote a well-known paper about the whole debate, called “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma.”

In 2023, cryptographer Filippo Valsorda organized a public bounty for anyone who could explain the seeds.

The story everyone believed

The best lead came from Jerry Solinas, a longtime NSA employee.

In 2015, he recalled that the seeds came from hashing a joke phrase. Something like “Give Bob and Jerry a raise.”

He couldn’t remember the exact words. The code was gone.

Solinas died in 2023.

So people kept guessing phrases and hashing them. Nothing matched.

What Claude did differently

In October 2026, an Anthropic employee asked an internal research model to try. This time, they did not give it the joke phrase hint.

According to Anthropic, Claude found the answer in under half an hour.

It didn’t chase the rumor.

It asked a different question: how would software in the 1990s have made random numbers?

Back then, a lot of C programs used simple built-in random number generators. They are fast, but weak. Weak means their output has patterns you can spot.

So Claude wrote a scanner to look for those patterns inside the seeds.

Then it noticed something.

Split into 32-bit chunks, four of the seeds had a zero as the top bit in every single chunk. Anthropic says the chance of that happening by luck is about 1 in 5,810.

That pattern is a fingerprint. The C function lrand48 only gives back 31 bits at a time, so the top bit is always zero.

From there, Claude worked out the generator’s hidden internal state. For some seeds that was a small brute force search. For others it used a known math method for this exact kind of problem, called lattice reduction (LLL).

Then it ran the generator backward.

At the start, it found Unix timestamps. A Unix timestamp is just the time on the computer’s clock, counted in seconds.

The prime curve seeds trace back to dates between May 1997 and April 1998.

In plain words: someone seeded a standard random number generator with the clock, and took the output.

That’s it.

Anyone can check it

This is the part I like most.

Anthropic published a short Python script. You give it the timestamp and the count, and it prints the exact published seed.

For P-256, that is the timestamp 1997–08–16 01:52:34 and candidate number 1,842.

Filippo Valsorda, who ran the bounty, says he rebuilt the method in Go to verify it.

So this isn’t “trust us.” It’s “run this.”

Why this makes the curves more trustworthy

A seed made from the clock leaves very little room to cheat.

Valsorda’s estimate is helpful here. Even if the NSA could pick any timestamp in 1997 and 1998, and any of the first 16 valid candidates, that’s only about 30 bits of freedom.

That sounds big. It isn’t.

To pick a weak curve with that little choice, weak curves would have to be very common. If that were true, all of elliptic curve crypto would be in trouble, and someone would likely have noticed in 25 years.

Anthropic’s own summary is calm: this is not a break, not a new attack, and there is nothing you need to change.

The bounty, $36,864, was donated to ISRG, the non-profit behind Let’s Encrypt.

What is still open

Anthropic was honest about the gaps, and I think that matters.

Some valid curves were skipped. For P-256, candidate 876 would also have worked. Nobody knows why it was passed over.

One binary curve seed, B-163, still fits nothing they tried.

The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 are still unexplained. A base point is the fixed starting point every key on that curve is built from.

Claude did explain the base points of six curves from May 1997. They came from the random number generator in an old math library called FreeLIP.

The pushback, fairly

Not everyone was impressed. The Hacker News thread had hundreds of comments. Here are the main points.

“This proves how they were made, not how they were chosen.” Some commenters said the NSA could still have searched over timestamps and kept the ones it liked.

The reply from cryptographers in the thread: with about 30 bits of choice, a targeted weak curve is very hard to believe.

“Most experts already trusted P-256.” True. Anthropic says this too. This was closing a chapter, not fixing a hole.

“Dual EC was the real backdoor.” Also true. But it’s a different standard, and it doesn’t make these curves guilty.

“A human with the right hunch could have done this.” Maybe. The method uses known tools. But nobody did it, partly because everyone trusted the joke phrase story.

“Claude learned from researchers’ papers and they don’t get credit.” This was a real debate in the thread, and it’s a fair question to ask about any AI result.

“This is a lab promoting its model.” Yes, partly. That’s why the reproducible script matters more than the press release.

The lesson for engineers

The win here was not a fancy new algorithm.

It was a better question.

People spent years asking “what was the phrase?” because someone they trusted said there was a phrase.

Claude asked “how did software work back then?”

That’s a habit worth stealing.

When you debug, the story you were told is a clue, not a fact.

Old systems usually did the simple, obvious thing.

And memory, even an expert’s, can be wrong.

Sometimes the mystery is just a timestamp.

Have you ever lost days on a bug because you trusted the explanation you were given?

Sources

  • Anthropic, “Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins” (Oct 16, 2026): https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins
  • Filippo Valsorda, “The NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty Has Been Claimed” (Oct 16, 2026): https://words.filippo.io/seeds-solved/
  • Hacker News discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122800
  • Koblitz and Menezes, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”: https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/1018
  • Steve Weis, “NIST curve seed origins”: https://saweis.net/posts/nist-curve-seed-origins.html

medium.titulo: Can Your IDE Catch Accessibility Issues Before QA?
medium.resumo: Bringing accessibility feedback closer to the code, without replacing human judgment.
medium.conteudo_html:
Bringing accessibility feedback closer to the code, without replacing human judgment.

Accessibility Shouldn’t Have to Wait for a Test Cycle

Picture a familiar scenario.

A developer finishes a feature, opens a pull request, and everything looks ready. The interface works, the API integration is complete, and the component behaves exactly as expected during mouse-based testing.

A few days later, QA identifies several accessibility issues.

A button cannot be reached using the keyboard. An icon-only control has no accessible name. A custom dropdown looks polished but does not communicate its expanded state to assistive technologies.

None of these problems necessarily requires a major architectural change. Yet fixing them late means reopening work, reviewing the implementation, repeating tests, and potentially delaying delivery.

What if developers received meaningful accessibility feedback while writing the component?

This is the question I have been exploring: Can we move accessibility feedback directly into the development environment, before a pull request even exists?

The Gap Between Writing Code and Validating Accessibility

Modern development environments are remarkably good at identifying problems early.

TypeScript catches type mismatches. ESLint flags suspicious patterns. Formatters enforce consistency. Framework tooling helps identify invalid usage and potential runtime issues.

Accessibility, however, is often treated differently.

Developers may rely on browser extensions, automated audits, QA processes, or accessibility specialists to identify issues after the interface has already been implemented.

These tools are valuable, but the feedback frequently arrives outside the moment when the developer is making the relevant decision.

Consider a simple Vue component:

<template>
  <div class="search-button" @click="openSearch">
    <SearchIcon />
  </div>
</template>

Visually, it might work perfectly.

From an accessibility perspective, though, it raises several questions:

  • Is the control keyboard accessible?
  • Does it expose the correct semantics?
  • Does it have an accessible name?
  • Can assistive technologies identify its purpose?

The better implementation is often straightforward:

<template>
  <button
    type="button"
    class="search-button"
    aria-label="Open search"
    @click="openSearch"
  >
    <SearchIcon aria-hidden="true" />
  </button>
</template>

The important difference is not the number of lines.

It is the engineering decision to use a native interactive element rather than recreate its behavior unnecessarily.

An IDE-based accessibility check could help surface that decision immediately.

What Static Analysis Can Actually Detect

Not every accessibility problem can be identified by inspecting source code.

However, many common patterns can be detected or flagged for review.

In Vue projects, useful checks might include:

1. Images without meaningful alternatives

<img :src="product.image" />

A tool can identify the missing alt attribute. It cannot automatically determine whether the image is informative or decorative.

2. Click handlers on non-interactive elements

<div @click="submitForm">
  Submit
</div>

This pattern deserves attention because keyboard interaction and semantic behavior may be missing.

3. Form controls without associated labels

<input v-model="email" type="email" />

An editor can flag the absence of an obvious accessible naming mechanism, while recognizing that some labels may be provided through component abstractions.

4. ARIA attributes with invalid values

<button aria-expanded="maybe">
  Options
</button>

Some ARIA attributes have explicitly defined allowed values. These are good candidates for deterministic validation.

5. Custom interactive components

Components that implement dialogs, menus, tabs, or comboboxes may require additional review of focus management, keyboard interaction, and state communication.

These examples suggest a useful distinction:

Static analysis can identify patterns and risks. It cannot establish that an entire user experience is accessible.

That limitation should shape how the tooling is designed.

Why Vue Makes This Interesting

Vue’s component architecture creates opportunities for accessibility checks, but also introduces challenges.

A component may receive its accessible name through a prop. Its underlying semantic element may be rendered dynamically. A reusable design-system component may encapsulate keyboard handling internally.

For example:

<BaseButton
  variant="primary"
  icon="search"
  label="Open search"
  @click="openSearch"
/>

Without understanding how BaseButton works, a simple analyzer might incorrectly flag this component.

The presence of a label prop does not automatically guarantee an accessible name, either. That depends on how the component renders it.

This is where developer tooling needs to become more context-aware.

A practical approach could combine:

  • Vue template parsing.
  • Rules for native HTML elements.
  • Knowledge of registered design-system components.
  • Configurable mappings for accessibility-related props.
  • Clear explanations of potential issues.
  • Suggestions that prioritize semantic HTML.

The objective should not be to generate as many warnings as possible.

It should be to deliver feedback developers can trust.

Where AI Can Help, and Where It Shouldn’t Decide

AI-assisted development adds another dimension.

Traditional static analysis works particularly well when rules are explicit and deterministic.

For example, checking whether aria-expanded contains a valid value does not require a language model.

But other questions are more contextual.

Does an image’s alternative text describe its purpose? Is a control’s accessible name meaningful? Does a proposed interaction pattern make sense for the user’s task?

AI may help developers investigate these questions by explaining context, proposing improvements, or highlighting potential concerns.

Still, an AI-generated recommendation is not equivalent to verified accessibility.

A useful model would separate three kinds of feedback:

Deterministic findings: Problems supported by explicit rules or reliably detectable patterns.

Contextual warnings: Potential issues requiring a developer to inspect surrounding behavior.

AI-assisted suggestions: Recommendations that may improve an implementation but require human validation.

This separation matters because confidence should be earned, not implied.

A developer should know whether a warning represents a confirmed rule violation or a hypothesis worth investigating.

Designing Feedback That Developers Will Actually Use

Developer experience is central to the effectiveness of any accessibility tool.

If an extension produces hundreds of noisy warnings, developers will eventually ignore them.

If it interrupts every keystroke, it becomes frustrating.

If it proposes unnecessary ARIA attributes, it may even encourage worse implementations.

A more useful experience would follow a few principles.

Explain the problem, not just the rule

Instead of displaying:

Accessibility violation: non-interactive element.

Explain:

This element handles a click event but may not support keyboard activation. Consider using a native button if the element performs an action.

Offer a practical next step

Warnings should help developers understand how to improve the code without automatically rewriting complex interactions.

Support progressive feedback

Lightweight checks can run while editing. More expensive analysis can run when saving a file, reviewing a component, or preparing a pull request.

Respect existing design systems

Organizations often have established component libraries. Tooling should understand those abstractions instead of treating every custom component as inherently inaccessible.

Avoid turning accessibility into a score

A single percentage can create a misleading impression of completeness.

Passing automated checks does not mean that keyboard navigation, screen reader interaction, cognitive accessibility, or the overall user experience has been adequately validated.

Exploring an Accessibility-First Developer Workflow

These ideas have led me toward an experimental direction I am calling AccessLens.

The concept is a developer-focused accessibility assistant that could integrate with environments such as VS Code and Cursor, initially concentrating on Vue components.

The goal would be to identify selected accessibility risks close to the source code and provide actionable, contextual feedback.

An initial exploration could focus on a small number of rules:

  • Native interactive semantics.
  • Accessible naming.
  • Image alternatives.
  • Selected ARIA validation.
  • Common keyboard accessibility risks.

More advanced capabilities, including design-system awareness and AI-assisted explanations, could be explored incrementally.

This is a research and prototyping direction, not a claim that a finished tool already exists.

The engineering challenge is not simply detecting patterns. It is determining which findings are reliable, which require context, and how to communicate that distinction clearly.

I am particularly interested in evaluating false positives, the usefulness of suggested fixes, and how early feedback changes the developer workflow.

Accessibility Is Still a Human Responsibility

Even with better tooling, accessibility cannot be reduced to automated validation.

A component may pass static checks and still be confusing to use.

A dialog may expose the correct roles while handling focus incorrectly.

A form may have labels but present error messages that are difficult to understand.

Meaningful accessibility evaluation still requires interaction testing, keyboard navigation, assistive technologies, and human judgment.

The purpose of earlier feedback is not to eliminate those practices.

It is to help developers address preventable issues sooner, so later testing can focus on more complex questions about real usability.

The Next Step Is Closer to the Code

In my previous articles, I explored why accessibility should become part of the development workflow and how Vue components can be designed with accessibility in mind.

The next question is how to make those principles easier to apply consistently.

For me, that means looking beyond another checklist or final-stage audit.

It means exploring tools that can recognize common risks, explain why they matter, and help developers make better decisions while the implementation is still taking shape.

The earlier we make accessibility visible, the more naturally it becomes part of engineering quality.

And perhaps the most useful accessibility warning is the one a developer receives before the problem ever reaches QA.

I’m a Senior Software Engineer and Tech Lead working across enterprise software, digital commerce, and accessible web experiences. I write about practical engineering approaches that help teams build more reliable, inclusive, and maintainable products.

medium.titulo: Wikinewsie (open-source bug) — Fix untranslated labels after switching languages
medium.resumo: In this article, I would like to write about a bug in Wikinewsie and how I tackled it.
medium.conteudo_html:
In this article, I would like to write about a bug in Wikinewsie and how I tackled it.

Here are a few quick things to know.

Wikinewsie is a web app that shows the most-edited Wikipedia.org articles over recent hours, automatically identifying current event topics and news that are undergoing active collaboration.

Wikimedia keeps its bug list on a website called Phabricator. Every bug gets a number starting with the letter T. Ours is T439940.

Here is the Open-source loop: Find a bug, make a branch, change the code, test it, save it, send it for review.

Fix untranslated labels in Wikinewsie after switching language: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough

The Bug Report:

Steps to replicate the issue (include links if applicable):

Open https://wikinewsie.toolforge.org/en
Use the language selector to pick another language (e.g., Polish)
What happens?:
Most of the elements are translated, but several are not.
In the Feed section -
*"Mix"
*"Editors"
*"Edits"

In the Mix weights section -

*"Edits"
*"Editors"
*"Growth"
*"Category"
*"New page"

What should have happened instead?:

These elements should have been shown in the newly selected language, instead of retaining the language of the initial selection.
Note that the bug doesn't appear when Polish interface is loaded directly, only when English is loaded first and then the language selector is used to switch to Polish.
Software version (on Special:Version page; skip for WMF-hosted wikis like Wikipedia):

Explaination:
On the Wikinewsie site, when someone opens the English version first and then uses the language dropdown to switch to Polish, most of the page changes to Polish, but a few words stay in English. Those words are:

  • In the Feed section: “Mix”, “Editors”, “Edits”
  • In the Mix weights section: “Edits”, “Editors”, “Growth”, “Category”, “New page”

Why does the bug matter? Think of a Polish reader. They pick Polish from the language dropdown and expect everything on the page in Polish. If a few buttons still say “Mix”, “Editors” and “Edits” in English, the page feels half-finished and confusing.

The plan

1. Make a new branch, so our work stays separate from the main code.
2. Find where the translations are stored.
3. Find which translation key belongs to each stuck label.
4. Find where the code uses those keys.
5. Work out why they do not update.
6. Fix it
7. Test it
8. Check that we changed only what we meant to change.
9. Commit, push, and open a merge request.

Switch to a new branch

git checkout -b fix-untranslated-labels-on-language-switch

Find where the translations are stored

Why we need it? Before fixing anything, we need to know where the words come from. We searched the whole project for one of the stuck labels.

grep -rni "mix weights" i18n src

What did we get?

./i18n/en.json:90:      "wikinewsie-mix-weights-label": "Mix weights:",

We learned two things from this:

1. The `i18n` folder holds the translations. (“i18n” is short for “internationalization”, which just means “making the app work in many languages”).

2. Think of it like a dictionary. The code asks for the key wikinewsie-mix-weights-label, and the language file hands back the right words Mix weights.

Find which translation key belongs to each stuck label.

We open the file i18/en.json and copy all the keys for the missing labels.

"wikinewsie-mix": "Mix",
"wikinewsie-edits": "Edits",
"wikinewsie-editors": "Editors",
"wikinewsie-growth": "Growth",
"wikinewsie-category": "Category",
"wikinewsie-new-page": "New page",

All six keys exist in the translation files. This confirms what the report hinted at: the translations are fine, so the problem must be in how the code uses them.

Find where the code uses these keys

We searched the `src` folder (where the app’s code lives) for the “Mix” key.

grep -rn "wikinewsie-mix'" src

The quote after the key makes it match wikinewsie-mix exactly, and not longer keys such as wikinewsie-mix-score

We found the culprit in src/App.vue :

const MODE_OPTIONS: Array<{ value: FeedMode; label: string; tooltip: string }> = [
  { value: 'score', label: text('wikinewsie-mix'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-mix-tooltip') },
  { value: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-editors-tooltip') },
  { value: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-edits-tooltip') },
];

Here is what each piece in that code is.

  • text('wikinewsie-mix') is the function that looks up a key and returns the words in the current language.
  • MODE_OPTIONS is the list of buttons for the Feed section.

Now the important part: when does text(…)run?

It runs once, at the moment the file loads and the list is created. At that moment the language is English, so the label is locked in as the plain word “Mix”. Later, when the user switches to Polish, the language changes, but this list is already built. Nobody rebuilds it. It keeps saying “Mix”.

It is like printing a menu. If you print it in English and the customer later asks for Polish, the printed menu does not change by itself. You have to print a new one.

Solution
Vue (the framework this app uses) has something called `computed` because of this Vue re-runs the whenever something it depends on changes.

We make the change to MODE_OPTIONS by adding computed

const MODE_OPTIONS = computed<Array<{ value: FeedMode; label: string; tooltip: string }>>(() => [
  { value: 'score', label: text('wikinewsie-mix'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-mix-tooltip') },
  { value: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-editors-tooltip') },
  { value: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-edits-tooltip') },
]);

What changed:

  • The list is wrapped in computed(() => [...])

So far, we have got MODE_OPTIONS labels (Mix, Editors, Edits) covered now.

We go on to the next labels for WEIGHTS(Edits, Editors, Growth, Category, New page)

We begin by searching for the keys that only this list uses

grep -n "wikinewsie-growth\|wikinewsie-category\|wikinewsie-new-page" src/App.vue

That led us to WEIGHTS_FIELDS. We checked where it is used and just as the previous one, we have to add computed

BEFORE:

const WEIGHT_FIELDS: Array<{ key: keyof ScoreWeights; label: string }> = [
  { key: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits') },
  { key: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors') },
  { key: 'growth', label: text('wikinewsie-growth') },
  { key: 'category', label: text('wikinewsie-category') },
  { key: 'isNew', label: text('wikinewsie-new-page') },
];

AFTER:

const WEIGHT_FIELDS = computed<Array<{ key: keyof ScoreWeights; label: string }>>(() => [
  { key: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits') },
  { key: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors') },
  { key: 'growth', label: text('wikinewsie-growth') },
  { key: 'category', label: text('wikinewsie-category') },
  { key: 'isNew', label: text('wikinewsie-new-page') },
]);
  • The list is now wrapped in computed(() => [...])

We saved the file, switched English to Polish in the running app, and both the Feed buttons and Weights buttons changed immediately to Polish.

Save the changes and Push

git add src/App.vue
git commit -m "Fix untranslated labels after switching language"
git push -u origin fix-untranslated-labels-on-language-switch

corrida_no_ar.titulo: BRASILEIRA AMADORA suspensa por DOPING na MARATONA de Buenos Aires
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Corredora amadora brasileira é pega no doping na Maratona de Buenos Aires. Atleta de elite etíope é suspensa por 6 anos por doping e fraude. Esclarecemos a lista de suspensões da ABCD e um médico explica o uso de testosterona em mulheres.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sexta-feira | 23 de outubro de 2026

Uma notícia que chamou a atenção foi o caso de doping da corredora amadora brasileira Laís Mascarenhas Gomes Araújo. Ela testou positivo para Drostanolona, um esteroide anabolizante mais conhecido como Masteron, durante a Maratona de Buenos Aires de 2024. A divulgação tardia do resultado, referente a uma prova do ano passado, levanta questões sobre os processos de análise. O Masteron é derivado da testosterona e é utilizado ilicitamente para ganho de massa magra, aumento de força e queima de gordura. Laís, que havia sido a quarta melhor brasileira na prova com o tempo de 3h06min21s, está agora sob suspensão provisória. Se a punição se tornar definitiva, todos os seus resultados desde a data do teste serão invalidados.

Etíope de elite é suspensa por 6 anos

A atleta de elite etíope Ruti Aga, vencedora da Maratona de Tóquio, foi suspensa por 6 anos. A punição se deve não apenas ao doping, com o uso da substância Metilprednisolona (um corticoide), mas também por fraude. Aga tentou justificar o uso apresentando uma prescrição médica falsa, assinada por um parente. A combinação de doping e tentativa de enganar as autoridades resultou em uma sanção severa, somando quatro anos pela fraude aos dois anos pelo uso da substância proibida.

Última etapa do ASICS Run Challenge em Florianópolis

O circuito ASICS Run Challenge, apresentado pelo Bradesco, está chegando à sua última etapa. Após passar por Belo Horizonte, Brasília, Fortaleza, Salvador e Recife, a prova final acontecerá em Florianópolis no dia 8 de novembro. Se você pretende participar, pode usar o cupom “CORRIDANOAR10” para garantir 10% de desconto na sua inscrição. O circuito, que conta com um ranking nacional para os 50 melhores atletas em cada distância, tem sido um sucesso e a expectativa é que continue crescendo.

Esclarecendo a lista de suspensos da ABCD

Recentemente, circulou um vídeo de um treinador que, ao analisar a lista de atletas suspensos pela ABCD (Autoridade Brasileira de Controle de Dopagem), interpretou erroneamente que os nomes destacados em amarelo seriam de atletas menores de idade. Na verdade, o destaque em amarelo apenas indica as atualizações mais recentes na lista. A legislação brasileira, especificamente o Código Brasileiro Antidopagem (CBA), proíbe a divulgação dos nomes de atletas menores de idade pegos no doping, mantendo esses casos em sigilo. Portanto, a informação de que a lista expunha menores não procede. O que a lista realmente mostra é um grande número de atletas de ciclismo e atletismo suspensos.

Médico fala sobre reposição de testosterona em mulheres

Em meio a tantos casos de doping, o médico Cadu Viterbo publicou um vídeo esclarecendo o uso de testosterona por mulheres. Ele explica que, diferente dos homens, não existe na literatura médica uma síndrome clínica definida por baixa testosterona em mulheres. A única indicação terapêutica aceita é para o transtorno do desejo sexual hipoativo, um caso muito específico. O uso para combater fadiga ou melhorar o desempenho não é reconhecido. Além disso, os exames laboratoriais comuns não têm a precisão necessária para diagnosticar uma deficiência em mulheres, cujos níveis são naturalmente baixos. Atletas que precisam usar substâncias proibidas para fins médicos devem solicitar uma Autorização de Uso Terapêutico (AUT) previamente à autoridade antidopagem, e não simplesmente apresentar uma receita depois.
